content: Specialist pediatric home-based nursing services have been suggested as a cost-effective approach to minimize the distress associated with hospital admissions. These services aim to improve primary care delivery and reduce the duration of hospital stays for children with acute and chronic illnesses. This review updates the original analysis published in 2006. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of specialist home-based nursing services for children with acute and chronic conditions. The evaluation focused on outcomes such as healthcare utilization, physical and mental health, patient and parental satisfaction, adverse health outcomes, and associated costs. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and Sociological Abstracts, was conducted in February 2012. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No language restrictions were applied during the search process. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children from birth to 18 years of age with acute or chronic illnesses. These children were assigned to receive either specialist home-based nursing care or conventional healthcare services. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, with discrepancies resolved by consulting a third author. Due to the clinical diversity of the studies and the lack of standardized outcome measures, meta-analysis was deemed inappropriate. Out of 4226 titles screened, seven RCTs involving a total of 840 participants were included in the review. The studies varied significantly in terms of participant characteristics, interventions, and outcomes. No significant differences in health outcomes were observed between the groups. However, two studies reported a reduction in the length of hospital stays without an increase in hospital readmission rates. Three studies noted a reduction in parental anxiety, and three studies reported improvements in child behavior. Additionally, three studies highlighted increased parental satisfaction with home-based care. One study reported better parental coping and improved family functioning. Conversely, one study found no effect on the parental burden of care, and another reported no impact on the functional status of children. In terms of costs, home-based care was found to be more expensive for service providers in two studies, but it resulted in substantial cost savings for families. However, one study reported no significant cost benefits for families. The authors concluded that current evidence does not support a reduction in hospital service utilization or hospital readmission rates for children with acute and chronic illnesses receiving specialist home-based nursing care. The only consistent finding across a few studies was a significant reduction in the length of hospital stays. Preliminary results indicated no adverse effects on physical health outcomes, and several studies reported improved satisfaction with home-based care. Further research is needed to evaluate health outcomes, satisfaction, healthcare utilization, and long-term costs associated with these services.
